title: Pollination and Fertilisation
tagline: How pollen reaches the stigma, the agents that carry it, and the double fertilisation unique to flowering plants.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every stage of pollen germination, double fertilisation and seed formation below is standard plant reproduction. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower, and fertilisation is the actual fusion of male and female gametes — two separate events that students routinely merge. This chapter keeps them apart. It defines pollination, contrasts self with cross pollination, and classifies pollination by the agent responsible: wind, water, insects or birds, with the flower's structure matched to whichever agent it relies on. It then follows a pollen grain all the way to the egg, through pollen-tube growth, the two male nuclei, the double fusion that gives angiosperms their name, and the ripening of the ovary into a fruit around the seeds.

facts.label: Pollination defined
facts.value: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma

facts.label: Double fertilisation
facts.value: One male gamete fuses with the egg, a second with the two polar nuclei

facts.label: Products
facts.value: Zygote to embryo; triple fusion gives endosperm; ovary to fruit; ovule to seed

facts.label: Seeds per ovule
facts.value: Each fertilised ovule becomes one seed

learningOutcomes: Define pollination and distinguish self pollination from cross pollination with their consequences for the offspring.
Classify flowers by their pollinating agent and relate each flower's structure to that agent.
Describe pollen germination and growth of the pollen tube to the ovule, and name the two fusion events of double fertilisation.
Explain how the ovary develops into a fruit and the ovule into a seed, and describe seed dispersal.

blocks.text: Pollination is simply the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower. It is a physical event and it does not involve any fusion at all; fusion is fertilisation, which happens much later and only if the pollen tube succeeds. When pollen moves within the same flower or between flowers on the same plant, it is self pollination, and it is cheap because no vector is needed, but it reduces variation because both gametes come from the same genetic background. When pollen moves between flowers on different plants of the same species, it is cross pollination, and it requires a vector plus structural adaptations, but it combines genes from two parents so the offspring show greater variation and vigour. Many plants have evolved devices specifically to prevent self pollination and force crossing, since a wider genetic spread gives the population a better chance of surviving disease and drought.

items: A cleistogamous flower never opens, so it must self pollinate and still set seed — the flower is closed but functional.
Cleistogamy is an advantage when pollinators are scarce, because the plant is guaranteed to produce seed.
Xenogamy is the term for cross pollination between two genetically different plants of the same species.
Geitonogamy is pollination between two flowers on the same plant: physically like self pollination but genetically close to it in effect.
Hybrid vigour, or heterosis, is the greater size and strength of cross-bred offspring.
Plants that self pollinate generation after generation gradually lose useful variations, which is why the devices preventing it matter.
Pollination is a transfer event; fertilisation is a fusion event — never use the two words interchangeably in an answer.
Pollen must land on a compatible stigma of the same species, otherwise it will not germinate at all.

items.text: Groundnut and some species of oxalis produce flowers below ground that never open; these cleistogamous flowers self pollinate in the bud and still give a good seed yield even where no insect visits.
items.note: A closed flower that still fruits is the evidence that pollination can happen without opening.

items.text: A gardener raises two lines of the same pea variety separately and then crosses them to obtain plants that are bigger and more uniform than either parent — the practical use of cross pollination.
items.note: This is the whole reason plant breeders control pollination by bagging flowers.

learn.title: Agents of pollination and the matching flower structure

blocks.text: Wind is the commonest agent of cross pollination, and wind-pollinated flowers are built for it rather than for show. They produce enormous quantities of tiny, smooth, lightweight pollen that stays airborne, their anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments so a breeze can shake the pollen free, and their stigmas are large, feathery and sticky so they can catch grains from the air. Petals are reduced to nothing or are small and dull, there is no scent and no nectar, because nothing needs to be attracted; grasses, maize, weeds and many trees follow this plan. Water pollination is rarer, seen in aquatic plants such as vallisneria and hydra, where the pollen is carried on the surface or just below it. Insect pollination is the reverse strategy: the flower is brightly coloured, scented, produces nectar and places pollen where it will stick to the insect's body, and the insect gets food in return. Bird pollination involves tubular red flowers with copious dilute nectar, since birds have poor smell but see red well.

blocks.caption: Flower adaptations by pollinating agent

Small or absent petals, no scent or nectar; long dangling anthers; large feathery stigmas
Light, often ribbon-shaped, carried on the surface
Flowers near or below the surface; stigma protruding to the water

Tubular red flowers with little scent, copious dilute nectar, strong stalks
Night-opening, pale, strongly scented, open bowl shape

items: Nectar guides are coloured lines or UV patterns on the petals that point the insect towards the nectary.
An insect-pollinated flower usually places pollen on the insect's back, where the stigma of the next flower will strike it.
Wind-pollinated flowers lack petals because colour is a costly advertisement with no customer.
Feathery stigmas and pendulous anthers are the two structural clues that instantly identify a wind-pollinated flower.
Sweet scent attracts insects by day; strong scent at night attracts moths, while a foul smell attracts flies.
A tubular flower with nectar at its base selects for a long-tongued insect, so the flower and its pollinator match one another.
Entomophily generally involves a reward — nectar, pollen, oil or a place to lay eggs — while some orchids deceive insects with no reward at all.
The reward system is what makes insects reliable visitors, and reliability is what makes cross pollination work.

items.text: A maize plant sheds kilograms of pollen per hectare into the air, and the silks of each kernel are long feathery stigmas designed to intercept those airborne grains.
items.note: Each silk leads to one ovule, so each pollen grain caught gives one kernel.

items.text: A honeybee entering a pea flower must prise open the keel, and as it does so the stamens spring up and dust pollen onto its abdomen; when it visits the next flower the stigma catches that same dust.
items.note: The pea flower's zygomorphic shape mechanically forces the transfer.

blocks.text: Plants that would otherwise self pollinate have evolved structural and temporal devices to avoid it, all of which come under the general idea of self-incompatibility or dichogamy. Temporal separation is the commonest: if the anthers of a flower mature before its stigma, the flower is protandrous, and cross pollination is forced because by the time the stigma is receptive the flower's own pollen is gone; if the stigma matures first the flower is protogynous, as in the fig and the mustard family. Spatial separation within one flower, called herkogamy, places the anthers and stigma at different heights or positions so that pollen cannot simply fall onto the stigma. Some flowers are heterostylous, producing two or three forms with styles and stamens of different lengths so that pollen from one form only fits the stigma of another. Many plants also have a genetic self-incompatibility in which the stigma refuses to germinate pollen from the same plant even when it lands there.

items.meaning: Maturation of the sexual organs at different times in the same flower, so self pollination is prevented.
The anthers shed pollen before the stigma becomes receptive.
The stigma becomes receptive before the anthers of the same flower shed pollen.
Spatial separation of anthers and stigma within a flower so pollen cannot reach the stigma directly.
Occurrence of two or more flower forms with styles and stamens of different lengths in one species.
A genetic block that stops pollen from germinating on a stigma of the same genetic constitution.

items: Unisexuality itself is a device: if a flower has only one sexual organ it cannot self pollinate.
A flower borne on a different plant from the pollen source removes self pollination even without any special structure.
Some plants shed pollen in the bud before the flower opens, so the pollen is gone by the time the stigma is exposed.
Waxy surfaces and sticky stigmas can reject incompatible pollen before it germinates.
Dichogamy is about time, herkogamy about position, and self-incompatibility about chemistry — the three are often confused.
Devices that promote cross pollination cost the plant more, so they are only worthwhile where they increase seed set or seed quality.
Where pollinators are scarce, a plant may retain cleistogamy as a reproductive insurance policy on the same individual.
Recognising the device in a question means first asking whether time, position or biochemistry is involved.

items.text: In many composites such as the dandelion, the style grows up through the ring of anthers, brushing pollen out onto itself before its own stigma lobes open and turn back on the pollen they carried up.
items.note: A single structure achieves export of the plant's pollen and then, later, reception of foreign pollen.

items.text: Two forms of the same primrose exist: one has a long style with short stamens, the other a short style with long stamens, so an insect picking up pollen from one form can only deposit it on the other.
items.note: Heterostyly makes incompatible pollen placement physically impossible rather than merely unlikely.

learn.title: Pollen germination, double fertilisation and fruit formation

blocks.text: Once a compatible pollen grain settles on the stigma it germinates: the grain swells, its exine splits, and a pollen tube grows out and forces its way down through the tissue of the style, nourished by the cells it digests. Inside the tube travel two male gamete nuclei and a tube nucleus. When the tube reaches the ovary it enters an ovule through a small opening called the micropyle and discharges its two male gametes into the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote — the first fertilisation. The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus — the second fusion, called triple fusion. Because two separate fusion events take place, the whole process is double fertilisation, and it is a defining feature of flowering plants. The zygote divides to form the embryo, the endosperm divides to form a food store, the ovule hardens into the seed, and the ovary wall thickens into the fruit that surrounds it.

blocks.caption: Events after the pollen tube arrives
rows: Develops into the embryo inside the seed
One male gamete + two polar nuclei
Develops into endosperm, the food store
Protects the seeds and aids dispersal
Degenerates once the gametes are discharged

items: Double fertilisation is the signature of angiosperms: two male gametes are used, one for the egg and one for the polar nuclei.
The endosperm is triploid, which lets it grow rapidly and build a large food reserve for the developing embryo.
The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle — this route is described as porogamy.
Synergids flank the egg and guide the pollen tube; the antipodals lie at the opposite end and degenerate.
Each ovule contains one embryo sac, and each fertilised ovule becomes one seed.
The fruit develops only from the ovary; any other part that swells, such as the thalamus in an apple, is an accessory structure.
A seedless fruit can still form — parthenocarpy produces bananas and grapes without fertilisation.
After fertilisation the sepals, petals and stamens usually wither and fall away.
Double fertilisation prevents the plant from wasting resources building endosperm in an ovule that was never pollinated.

items.text: In wheat, one pollen grain germinates on each stigma and sends a tube down the style; the resulting zygote becomes the embryo, the triploid endosperm becomes the floury part of the grain, and the ovary wall fuses with the seed coat to give a dry one-seeded fruit.
items.note: The wheat grain is the standard example of a caryopsis, where fruit and seed cannot be separated.

items.text: A maize kernel set without pollination stays small and shrivels, while a pollinated kernel fills out; the difference is the endosperm, which only forms after triple fusion.
items.note: Commercial sweetcorn is often sold unpollinated, which is why the kernels are uniformly small and tender.

keyPoints: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; it is not the fusion of gametes.
Self pollination is cheap but produces little variation; cross pollination needs a vector but gives variation and hybrid vigour.
Cleistogamous flowers never open and always self pollinate, which guarantees seed even without pollinators.
Wind-pollinated flowers have abundant light pollen, dangling anthers, feathery stigmas, and no showy petals or scent.
Insect-pollinated flowers are coloured, scented and nectar-producing, and place pollen where it will stick to the visitor.
Dichogamy separates the sexes in time, herkogamy separates them in position, and self-incompatibility blocks them chemically.
The pollen tube grows from the stigma down the style and enters the ovule at the micropyle.
Double fertilisation = one male gamete with the egg giving a diploid zygote, plus one male gamete with two polar nuclei giving a triploid endosperm nucleus.
The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit; each fertilised ovule gives one seed.
Parthenocarpy produces fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless bananas and grapes.
examFocus: Never call pollination fertilisation. Pollination is a transfer, fertilisation is a fusion; mixing the words loses the mark for the definition even when the rest of the answer is right.
Double fertilisation answers must name both fusion events and both products — zygote and triploid endosperm nucleus — because the second fusion is what the term refers to.
Agent questions want a matched pair: name the agent, then give two structural adaptations of the flower that suit it, not adaptations of two different agents.
Seed and fruit formation is asked as a sequence, so give it in order: pollen tube, two fusions, zygote and endosperm, ovule to seed, ovary to fruit.

options: Fusion of the male and female gametes inside the ovule
Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma
Growth of the pollen tube down the style
Development of the ovary into a fruit
questions.answer: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma
questions.explanation: Pollination is purely the physical movement of pollen from an anther to a receptive stigma. Fusion of gametes is fertilisation, the growth of the pollen tube is pollen germination, and the swelling of the ovary is fruit formation — three later events that must not be used as the definition.
questions.commonMistake: Using the word fertilisation in the definition of pollination, which is the single most common error in this chapter.

questions.prompt: The fusion of one male gamete with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus is called __________ fusion, and together with the fusion with the egg it makes __________ fertilisation.
questions.explanation: Three nuclei take part in the second fusion — one male gamete and two polar nuclei — which is why it is triple fusion. Since this and the fusion of the male gamete with the egg are two separate fusion events, the whole process is called double fertilisation, a feature unique to flowering plants.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the two terms. Triple fusion is the second event; double fertilisation is the name for the pair of events.

questions.prompt: Which combination of features is characteristic of a wind-pollinated flower?
options: Brightly coloured petals, sweet scent and abundant nectar
Large quantities of light pollen, dangling anthers and feathery stigmas
Tubular red corolla with copious dilute nectar
Spiny pollen and a strong odour of decay
questions.answer: Large quantities of light pollen, dangling anthers and feathery stigmas
questions.explanation: Wind pollination needs pollen that will stay airborne and a stigma large enough to intercept it, so the plant makes vast amounts of tiny dry pollen, hangs its anthers out where a breeze can shake them, and gives the stigma a feathery surface. Petals, scent and nectar belong to insect-pollinated flowers, the tubular red form to bird pollination, and the decaying odour to fly pollination.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option with abundant nectar, which describes insect or bird pollination — wind cannot be bribed with food.

questions.prompt: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of cross pollination compared with self pollination.
questions.answer: Advantage: cross pollination brings together genes from two different parents, so the offspring show greater genetic variation and can be better adapted to a changing environment. Second advantage: the offspring often show hybrid vigour, growing more strongly and uniformly than the selfed line, which is why plant breeders use it. Disadvantage: it is expensive and unreliable, because the plant must produce showy petals, scent and nectar to attract a vector, and seed set depends on that vector actually visiting — if pollinators are absent, no seed forms at all.
questions.explanation: Two advantages and one disadvantage are asked for, and each must be tied to a cause: variation comes from combining two gene pools, vigour from heterozygosity, and the cost from needing a vector. Stating only that cross pollination 'gives better offspring' without explaining the genetic reason earns partial credit.
questions.commonMistake: Counting 'variation' and 'hybrid vigour' as the same point. They are related but separately argued, and the question asks for two.

questions.prompt: Describe the events from the arrival of a pollen grain on a compatible stigma to the formation of the embryo and the food store, making clear the two fusion events involved.
questions.answer: The pollen grain lands on a receptive stigma and germinates: it absorbs moisture, the exine splits, and a pollen tube grows out and bores down through the style, its tip carrying a tube nucleus and two male gamete nuclei. On reaching the ovary the tube enters an ovule through the micropyle and discharges the two male gametes into the embryo sac. The first fusion occurs when one male gamete unites with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, which divides and develops into the embryo. The second fusion occurs when the other male gamete unites with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which divides to become the endosperm, the food reserve that nourishes the developing embryo. These two successive fusion events constitute double fertilisation.
questions.explanation: The answer must be told as a sequence with both fusions named and both products stated. The route through the style and the micropyle shows understanding of the pathway, while the two products — diploid zygote and triploid endosperm — show understanding of what double fertilisation actually means.
questions.commonMistake: Naming only the fusion with the egg. The term double fertilisation specifically requires the second fusion with the polar nuclei to be described.

questions.prompt: A flower whose anthers shed pollen three days before its stigma becomes receptive is showing which device against self pollination?
questions.explanation: Dichogamy is separation in time, and when the male part matures first it is specifically protandry — proto meaning first and andr referring to the male organ. By the time the stigma is receptive the flower's own pollen has already gone, so only pollen arriving from elsewhere can fertilise it. Herkogamy separates the parts in position, heterostyly involves different flower forms, and cleistogamy is a permanently closed flower.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing herkogamy because both terms sound technical. Herkogamy is about position, whereas this question is entirely about timing.

questions.prompt: A plant produces small green flowers with no scent, anthers that dangle well outside the flower on long filaments, stigmas that are large and feathery, and pollen that is smooth, dry and produced in very large amounts. Identify the agent of pollination, and explain how four separate features of the flower are adaptations to that agent. State one cost this plant avoids by not attracting animals.
questions.answer: The agent is wind. The four adaptations are: first, pollen is produced in enormous quantity because most grains never reach a stigma, so sheer numbers compensate for the waste; second, the pollen is smooth, dry and lightweight so it remains airborne instead of clumping; third, the anthers dangle outside the flower on long filaments so that any breeze can shake the pollen free; and fourth, the stigma is large and feathery, giving a broad net-like surface that can catch grains from the air. The cost avoided is producing a showy corolla, scent and nectar — resources that would be wasted on wind, which cannot be attracted, and which can instead be diverted into making more pollen.
questions.explanation: Each of the four features must be tied to a specific problem of wind pollination: waste, buoyancy, release and capture. The final part asks for a cost argument, so it must name the structures not built and explain why building them would be pointless for an abiotic vector.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the four features without explaining the problem each solves. The question asks for adaptations, which means structure linked to function, not structure alone.

questions.prompt: State what each of the following becomes after fertilisation: the ovule, the ovary, the zygote, and the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
questions.answer: The ovule becomes the seed, with its integuments hardening into the seed coat. The ovary wall develops into the fruit that encloses the seeds. The zygote divides repeatedly to form the embryo, which becomes the new plantling inside the seed. The triploid primary endosperm nucleus divides to form the endosperm, the nutritive tissue that feeds the developing embryo.
questions.explanation: All four must be given because each pair — ovule and ovary, zygote and endosperm — tests a different level of the same sequence. The two most commonly confused are the zygote becoming the embryo and the endosperm becoming the food store; naming the seed coat as the fate of the integuments adds precision.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the ovule becomes the fruit. The ovule becomes the seed, and it is the ovary that becomes the fruit.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a true fruit?
options: An apple, developing mainly from the thalamus
A strawberry, with seeds on its surface
A mango, developing only from the ovary wall
A fig, which is a hollow receptacle bearing flowers inside
questions.answer: A mango, developing only from the ovary wall
questions.explanation: A true fruit develops solely from the ovary, and the mango is the standard example: its fleshy part and its stone are both ovary wall and seed. The apple develops largely from the swollen thalamus, the strawberry carries its achenes on an enlarged receptacle, and the fig is a hollow inflorescence structure, so all three are false or accessory fruits.
questions.commonMistake: Calling a fruit false simply because it has a stone or many seeds. What makes a fruit true is which floral part it develops from.

questions.prompt: The pollen tube enters the ovule through a small opening called the __________, and the tissue that surrounds and protects the developing embryo, formed from the outer layers of the ovule, is called the __________.
questions.explanation: The micropyle is the pore left in the ovule's integuments, and it is the route by which the pollen tube reaches the embryo sac; after fertilisation it often remains as a small scar on the seed and still allows water to enter during germination. The integuments of the ovule harden and dry into the seed coat, which protects the dormant embryo against mechanical damage and loss of water.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'endosperm' for the second blank. The endosperm is the food store; the protective covering is the seed coat.

questions.prompt: A farmer notices that a field of a self-pollinating crop sets seed well even in a week when almost no insects are seen. Suggest an explanation, describe one structural feature that ensures this happens, and state one disadvantage the farmer might face over several seasons of the same practice.
questions.answer: The crop must be self pollinating, and the reliable seed set with few insects shows that it does not depend on a vector for reproduction. A common structural basis is cleistogamy, in which some or all flowers never open, so the anthers and stigma lie close together inside the closed bud and pollen reaches the stigma directly; because the flower is enclosed, no insect visit is needed and the flower is protected from rain as well. The disadvantage over several seasons is the loss of genetic variation: self pollination combines genes from the same genetic background each generation, so any harmful recessive alleles are not diluted out and the plants become increasingly uniform, making the whole crop vulnerable to a single disease or to a change in growing conditions.
questions.explanation: The observation must first be linked to the absence of a vector requirement, then to a specific structure such as cleistogamy, and finally to the long-term genetic cost. The third part asks for a consequence over generations, so it must address variation and uniformity rather than simply repeating that self pollination occurs.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping after describing cleistogamy. The disadvantage over seasons is a separate argument about genetic variation, and it carries its own marks.
